utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. My apologies for a slight delay -- actually, I entered the wrong courtroom. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honour. This is Case Number IT-03-68-PT, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Will both parties make their appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. For the Prosecution team my name is Jan Wubben, senior trial attorney; co-counsel, Gramsci Di Fazio; legal officer, Kristina Carey, together with Deanna Boles, case manager. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I note Mr. Jayasuriya has been replaced?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Not yet, but he couldn't attend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon or good day, Your Honours. My name is Vasvija Vidovic, and together with my colleague John Jones we are representing Mr. Oric. Ms. Jasmina Cosic is also with us as our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic. This is the fourth Status Conference held in accordance with Rule 65 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Thanks to the incredible diligence of both parties, I'm now pleased to inform the parties that this is -- this case is ready for trial and actually has been scheduled to commence soon after the summer recess. With the permission of the President of the International Tribunal, I can tell you now that this case is to be heard by one of the sections of Trial Chamber II being presided by the Honourable Judge Carmel Agius. And Judge Agius kindly indicated to me that the pre-trial conference could be held early in the week of 27th of September, 2004 with the full trial commencing the following week as early as 4th of October, 2004. So I would like to hear from the parties if there's any problem in having a pre-trial conference on Tuesday, 28th of September, 2004, and the trial starting on next Tuesday, 5th of October, 2004. I see no objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour. In addition, I would like to make a remark, because we indicated through our contacting with a group of more than 30 witnesses, that last week they didn't have a passport yet, and so we processed it. And due to the cooperation with police authorities, they will see to it that it will be processed and there's supported. And an estimation is that they will need six weeks, so that should be fine, and I indicate no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Having set the trial date, this case will be given some sort of priority, and I encourage you to do your best to get ready. And I see no objections from the Defence either. So it will be so ordered. Having said that, then, I would like to wrap up briefly the current state of the case. There's a pending motion with respect to Prosecution's requesting to add two witnesses. My understanding is that there's no objection from the Defence on this. So the motion is hereby granted. In general, the pre-trial preparations with respect to disclosure under Rule 66 and 68 and everything has been going have been smoothly. Before we deal with the disclosure matter, I understand that there's an issue raised by the Prosecution to intend to add to their list of witnesses some ten witnesses. So can I hear -- can we hear the start from the matter. Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for raising this issue, because after the -- after Monday, the 65 ter conference, we prepared to submit more information in that regard. On Monday we stated that we intended to seek permission to add approximately 10 to 15 new witnesses to the Prosecution's witness list. During that Status Conference, concerns had been expressed about the total number of witnesses sought to be added and the possibility that these witnesses and their companion evidentiary material might cause delay to the commencement of trial. To facilitate an early trial date and to prevent an unnecessary delay, the Prosecution has reviewed its proposed group of potential witnesses that it wishes to add to the list and has reduced the number to six witnesses; however, we will seek to obtain two further witnesses, and I will provide details of that couple later on in my submission. So back to the reduced list of six witnesses. Two of those projected six witnesses are forensic handwriting and document experts who will give evidence as to the authenticity and authorship of documents on the Prosecution's exhibit list. Defence counsel has been provided with a courtesy copy of their first and principle report with a second supplementary report to be delivered to the Defence this week. The Defence has expressed its intention to challenge the authenticity of documents on the Prosecution's exhibit list. These two experts will assist the Trial Chamber in determining the question of authenticity. The Defence has expressed its intention to call its own forensic handwriting and document expert. Of that list of six witnesses, three additional witnesses will be called to establish the fact of the death of three of the victims identified in the amended indictment, so included in the charges. The Prosecution has offered the Defence the opportunity to stipulate to the fact that the victims identified in the indictment are deceased, but the Defence has declined to do so. This necessitates calling relatives of the deceased to prove the fact of death. The final witness, number six, will be called to authenticate radio message intercepts. These intercepts will be provided to the Defence. A subsequent motion will seek permission to add these intercepts to the Prosecution's list of exhibits. However, that intercept witness, number six, can only authenticate four out of the 17 intercepts the Prosecution will seek to produce into evidence. This witness has already agreed to provide a statement simply on the issue of authentication. Therefore, the Prosecution will seek to call additional witnesses, two witnesses, to prove the remainder of the intercepts. It is intended that these two witnesses will be purely formal witnesses whose evidence will be very brief just to prove the remaining evidence. It may be that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Wubben, I'm sorry to interrupt you but let me be clear about this thing. Two additional witnesses, two further witnesses, are they included in six or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: They are not included in six.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. This is in addition to six, you may wish to call two further witnesses to --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the -- to prove authenticity of the intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: But I'd like to inform you that we will file a motion in that regard of those two -- six witnesses, and it means that in the future we might get back to an additional opportunity of two witnesses. This is to inform you that it may well be that Defence counsel will not dispute authenticity of the intercepts, in which case these intercept witnesses will not be called at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. But before I hear from the Defence I would like to encourage you to file your motion as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: We will, Your Honour. We will file this seeking -- this allowance to add those witnesses at the end of the week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Vidovic, do you have -- Mr. Jones, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Well, to a certain extent this may be a matter now which is for Trial Chamber II to decide when the Prosecution brings a motion. So I make three brief points, three brief observations. Starting from the general moving to the particular. The general points --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. But this Trial Chamber can look into the matter. It is for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Your Honour. Firstly, dealing with the statute and the right of the accused to a fair trial, I'll just make the following point: That as far as any claimed right or any right claimed by the Prosecution to bring witnesses at any stage is concerned, that is obviously subject to the right of an accused to a fair trial guaranteed by Article 21 of the statute. And if at the 11th hour new witnesses are going to be introduced, new evidence, new points, new issues, then obviously that raises the prospect that the accused's right to a fair trial may be jeopardised, given that he may not have the adequate time and facilities to prepare on those points. As far as authenticity of documents is concerned, obviously we have raised this issue, and it's reasonable for the Prosecution to find witnesses to deal with that point. So my point really goes to the other witnesses whom the Prosecution intends to call. Turning to the Rules of Procedure and Evidence next. Rule 66 and Rule 65 ter contemplate an orderly procession, if you like, of various Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond stages of the pre-trial stage being completed whereby the Prosecution files its list of witnesses it intends to call, it has to serve the statements on the Defence by certain dates. And so for the Prosecution to claim, if they are so claiming, that new statements may be introduced willy-nilly whenever they like, then that would upset the whole logic of the rules. It would upset the economy and rationale of the rules and would make of the rules a charade. We have reached the stage where, as Your Honour has observed, due to diligence on both sides, we are now trial ready and the introduction of new evidence would threaten to upset that stage we have finally reached. And indeed it would be impossible for us ever to really say that we are trial ready if the Prosecution will keep introducing evidence at different stages of the proceedings. As far as the evidence concerning evidence of death of victims is concerned, this is something which right from the start the Prosecution would anticipate would be necessary as part of their case, their case being that these victims died. And so as far as the notion that the Defence could have stipulated to the death of the victims, it is something obviously which is out of the Defence's knowledge, and it was something which the Prosecution always anticipated, as long as a year or a year and a half ago, that they would need to call those witnesses. And so it's my submission it would be extremely late in the day for the Prosecution to seek to prove those points, and it's certainly wrong to suggest that it's due to a failure by the Defence to stipulate to such a controversial point that the Prosecution now has to prove that point. And then finally, just dealing very specifically with the orders which Your Honour has issued in this case. Your Honour has been issuing orders with deadlines for the service of documents. For example, Your Honour's order of the 30th of July, 2003, which dealt, inter alia, with the filing of Rule 66(A)(ii) statements and expert reports, and a date which was set in that order was the 14th of November, 2003, which I believe was later extended. And then at the Status Conference of the 28th of November, 2003, Your Honour ordered that all materials under Rule 66(A)(ii) would be filed by the 16th of January this year, with the exception of certain specified materials. And I certainly, or we certainly understand that to mean everything referred to in Rule 66(A)(ii), which would include additional statements, additional Prosecution statements, in the second clause of 66(A)(ii). And so in my submission, it would make a mockery of those orders if, again, more and more witnesses were to be introduced at such a late stage. And the Prosecution certainly, it appears, understood your order in that sense, that they would have to seek leave in order to add any additional witnesses, because indeed in the Prosecution motion, for example, of the 12th of May, 2004, to add witnesses, the Prosecution referred to Your Honour's order and sought leave to add new witnesses. So certainly the Prosecution recognises that this is outside -- this would be outside the deadlines which have been set for filing additional evidence. So in conclusion, Your Honour, the Prosecution can make its application, and it will be a matter for the Trial Chamber to rule upon. But our position, apart from the witnesses dealing with the issue of authenticity, which we recognise is new, is something which we will vigorously oppose, not least because we will already have to deal with five anonymous witnesses whose statements we will receive unredacted in full only 30 days before the trial starts. We will have to be making inquiries and dealing with those matters. And so to have to deal with other witnesses dealing with, as I say, new issues, new evidence, then that could really put us in a difficult position. But that's just to give us an indication of the Defence's position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Having heard your points, can I ask you -- if we receive the Prosecution's motion by the end of this week, when do you think you can file your response to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would imagine fairly rapidly. I would imagine within five days certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then the next matter would be 92 bis witnesses. And my understanding is that the parties agreed -- the Defence agreed to admission of one statement without cross-examination and the other six. So therefore the Prosecution is planning to call them in the form of 98 -- 89(F) or something like that. Am I right in this?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we consider to make use of 89(F) due to expedited trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: However, even if that was agreed by the parties, I would like the parties to file their motions and response formally so that the actual Trial Chamber which is to hear the case to be able to look into the matter, and it's up to them whether they can admit the 92 bis without cross-examination, despite some opposition from the Defence. So I like to -- I like the motion and response to be filed formally. Can it be done? Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, you are now referring to 89(F)?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Or 92 bis. Or, in the alternative, 89(F).

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I'll see to it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I mentioned the very smooth proceeding in relation to disclosure matter. If there's anything the parties may raise in relation to disclosure, I'd like to hear from the Prosecution. None?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Jones mentioned that this unredacted disclosure -- disclosure of unredacted statements of protected witnesses, that's five in number. So those statements in unredacted form should be disclosed prior to -- 30 days prior to the commencement of the date. Now the trial date is set, so there should be no problem in disclosing those witnesses' statements. No. And I noticed that the Defence -- the Defence's opposition, objection to the military -- in regard to -- in relation to military expert. Their opposition as to the qualification and the area of expertise still stands?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that remains our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That can be dealt with by this Chamber or the Trial Chamber II, which is to hear the case. Is there any other matter to be raised by the parties at this time?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. No thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Oric, do you want to say anything in relation to your status or your detention? Anything?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have nothing to say, Your Honour. Everything is in good order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then this hearing is adjourned.
